query_text: how do bacteriophages differ from antibiotics

content.text:
Bacteriophages (“phages”) and antibiotics both can be used against bacterial infections, but they work very differently.

| Feature | Bacteriophages | Antibiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **What they are** | Viruses that infect bacteria | Chemical drugs, natural or synthetic |
| **Target** | Usually very specific bacterial strains or species | Often broader groups of bacteria |
| **How they kill/inhibit bacteria** | Attach to bacteria, inject genetic material, replicate, and often burst the bacterial cell | Interfere with bacterial processes such as cell-wall synthesis, protein synthesis, DNA replication, or metabolism |
| **Specificity** | Highly specific; may kill only the target bacterium | Can be broad-spectrum or narrow-spectrum |
| **Effect on microbiome** | Usually less disruptive because they target specific bacteria | Can disrupt normal beneficial bacteria, especially broad-spectrum antibiotics |
| **Resistance** | Bacteria can become resistant to phages, but phages can also evolve in response | Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics, and the drug itself does not evolve |
| **Replication** | Can multiply at the infection site if target bacteria are present | Do not replicate; concentration depends on dosing and metabolism |
| **Use in medicine** | Used in some countries and studied as alternatives or complements to antibiotics | Widely used standard treatment worldwide |
| **Limitations** | Need correct phage matched to the bacterial strain; immune system may clear them; regulatory/production challenges | Resistance, side effects, allergies, microbiome disruption |

In short: **antibiotics are chemical agents that broadly or specifically inhibit bacteria, while bacteriophages are bacteria-infecting viruses that usually target very specific bacteria and can replicate where those bacteria are present.**
